books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Grover Cleveland, veto message on the Texas Seed Bill, February 16, 1887

stimulus.text:
President Grover Cleveland, veto message on the Texas Seed Bill, February 16, 1887. Congress had voted $10,000 to buy seed grain for Texas farmers after a drought.

“I can find no warrant for such an appropriation in the Constitution, and I do not believe that the power and duty of the General Government ought to be extended to the relief of individual suffering which is in no manner properly related to the public service or benefit. A prevalent tendency to disregard the limited mission of this power and duty should, I think, be steadfastly resisted, to the end that the lesson should be constantly enforced that, though the people support the Government, the Government should not support the people.”
stimulus.source_note: Grover Cleveland, veto message, February 16, 1887 (American Presidency Project transcript). The quoted sentences are exact; the $10,000 appropriation and the drought are stated in the message.

stem: According to Cleveland, why did he veto the bill?

options.text: Texas farmers had asked for too little money
options.misconception: Cleveland never says the sum was too small; he objects to the spending itself.

options.text: The drought in Texas had already ended
options.misconception: Cleveland admits the suffering was real and the need was genuine.

options.text: The Constitution gives no warrant for federal relief of individual suffering
Only the states could buy seed grain for Texas farmers
options.misconception: Cleveland says the relief should come from private charity, not that only states could buy seed.

rationales.A: Cleveland objects to the appropriation itself, not to the size of the sum.
rationales.B: Cleveland admits the need was real, so the drought had not ended.
rationales.C: Cleveland says he can find no warrant for the spending in the Constitution.
rationales.D: Cleveland points to private charity, not to state governments, as the proper source of relief.
rationales.general:
Take the reason from his own words.
1. Cleveland says he can find no warrant for the spending in the Constitution.
2. He says the power of the government should not reach relief of individual suffering.
3. He admits the farmers truly suffered, so need alone did not decide him.
4. The veto rests on the Constitution and the limits of government, not on the sum.
Remember: a veto message states its reason, so quote the reason, not the sympathy.
